results.corrected_extracted: General-population sample: NLAES (1991–1992, response 90%) and NESARC (2001–2002, response 81%) pooled; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18–57 in five 10-year birth cohorts (born 1934–1943 to 1974–1983), 4,603 to 16,329 per cohort; people older than 57 and people born outside the US excluded; lifetime drinkers had had more than 12 drinks; ages at first drink, at onset of DSM-IV alcohol dependence (AUDADIS-IV) and at first alcohol treatment were all recalled at one interview.
results.note: The smallest cohort is born 1934–1943 (n = 4,603); 5,845 is the 1974–1983 cohort. Range is 4,603–16,329, and the cohort ns sum to 53,238. Everything else matches. 'Recalled' follows from the cross-sectional design (Discussion, 6th paragraph).

Matches the Discussion's sensitivity analysis. Only cohorts in both surveys (born 1944–1973) can be compared. The closing clause is the card's appraisal, labelled as such; the authors read the check as showing limited recall bias.

Matches the three sources of bias in paragraphs 1–3. Here the AA convenience sample is 'mostly male', and that point is attributed to other scholars. Magnification and accelerated progression are as printed.

Matches. 3rd paragraph: discard the term and the 'masculine' framework; study intersections with race, class, age, education and culture. 4th paragraph: design studies from the outset rather than underpowered post hoc analyses (following DeBruin); use descriptive rather than comparative language.
